name: Hana Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for taking the time, Hana. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the fault and emergency crew for the coast district, so my day depends on what breaks. I work a rota, days one week, nights the next. A quiet shift is planned jobs, replacing corroded fittings, because the salt off the sea eats everything. A busy one is a car into a pole at two in the morning, or a line down across the seafront road in a gale.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the live-line work, doing medium-voltage jobs with rubber gloves and sleeves, without switching the street off. It's slow and exact, and people's fridges keep running. What wears me out is the rota. Marcus works regular hours at the distribution warehouse, so on night weeks we pass each other in the hall like flatmates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, that's what I expected. I'd probably say it in the crew room and leave it there. I'm not a big online person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be a bit of a relief, mostly for Marcus. His warehouse has been testing robot pickers and everyone there's been jumpy. If it all fizzles, he's safe and so am I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep saving, we've got about eight months put by and Marcus has a decent pension. Keep using the AI app now and then, I use it to explain Kai's maths homework because I've forgotten all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved for the house more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the jumpiness at Marcus's warehouse look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rumours in the canteen, mostly. A robot picker did a trial on one aisle in the summer and kept dropping boxes of tinned tomatoes. Everyone laughed, but they also went quiet. Marcus came home and said, they'll fix it, and then what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who comes out ahead in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nobody much, which is fine by me. Some software firms got rich on the hype. I'm in the middle on most things, I don't think it's a scandal, it's just how money works.

S0.say: I'd say that's about what I expected and mention it in the crew room, then leave it there, since I'm not much of an online person.
S0.think: It would be a relief, mainly for my partner, whose warehouse has been testing robot pickers. If AI fizzles, both our jobs are safe.
S0.do: Carries on as now, adding to about eight months of savings on top of her partner's pension. Keeps using an AI app now and then, for instance to explain her son's maths homework.
S0.feel: Calm, relieved for the household more than for herself.
S0.quote: A robot picker did a trial on one aisle in the summer and kept dropping boxes of tinned tomatoes. Everyone laughed, but they also went quiet.
S0.fieldNote: From the start, Hana's thinking runs through her partner's warehouse job, which feels more exposed than hers. She's a light, practical AI user. Her political view is shrugging and middle-of-the-road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change a lot of jobs and we'd better be sensible about it. Train people, don't just bin them. That's what I'd say if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is fine for a good while, a robot isn't doing glove work on a wet pole in a gale. Marcus's is the worry. In this picture his warehouse goes half robots in a few years, and he'd be managing machines instead of people, or not managing at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Marcus and look at what he could move into, maybe the robot side, maybe something else. I'd use the AI stuff at work more once the crew's figured out which bits actually help. And I'd keep saving, maybe a bit more, in case he has a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. For him more than for me. It's hard watching someone you love get nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that conversation with Marcus look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kitchen table, Sunday, after the kids are in bed. Laptop open, me asking the AI what warehouse managers move into, him rolling his eyes. Then actually reading it. That's how we do most big things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for the crew to figure out which tools help. Who figures that out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ollie, usually. He's the one who tries everything and tells us what's rubbish. I'm happy to be second or third. I don't need to be first, I need it to work at two in the morning.

S1.say: I'd say lots of jobs will change and we need to be sensible, training people instead of throwing them away.
S1.think: My job is safe for a good while because no robot is doing glove work on a wet pole in a gale. My partner's warehouse job is the real worry if it goes half robots.
S1.do: Sits down with her partner to map out jobs he could move into. Uses AI tools at work more once the crew has found what helps, and saves a bit more in case he has a gap between jobs.
S1.feel: Uneasy for her partner more than for herself.
S1.quote: I don't need to be first, I need it to work at two in the morning.
S1.fieldNote: Her concern is almost entirely for her partner. She'd use AI to help him plan, which shows her steady comfort with it. She is content to let a tech-keen colleague test tools before she relies on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's driving the bus. Not the companies, not the government, nobody. I'd say that in the crew room and to my mum on the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. Marcus would probably be out within a year. I'd last a bit longer, but two years for robots to do my job too, I honestly don't know if that's possible, and I don't like not knowing. Eight months of savings would go fast with one wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut things the first month: the caravan holiday, the kids' music lessons we could pause. I'd put more into savings and overpay the mortgage while I've got the wage. I'd talk to my parents, they've got a paid-off house with a spare room, about being a safety net if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Tight in the chest. But I'd still feel like I could steer, just about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pause the music lessons. How would you explain that to the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lily's fifteen, she'd understand, she'd probably offer before I asked. Kai would be upset. I'd tell him it's a break, not the end, and I'd mean it. He'd keep his guitar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you like to wait until something's proven. What happens to that with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't work. By the time it's proven, it's done. That's what scares me most, I'm a wait-and-see person in a picture where waiting means you've already lost.

S2.say: I'd say nobody is driving the bus, not companies and not government, and I'd tell that to the crew room and to my mum on the phone.
S2.think: It frightens me, because my partner would likely be out within a year and I don't know whether my job would follow. Eight months of savings goes fast on one wage.
S2.do: Cuts the caravan holiday and pauses the children's music lessons in the first month. Saves more and overpays the mortgage while she has a wage, and asks her parents about their spare room as a fallback.
S2.feel: Anxious and tight in the chest, but still feeling she can just about steer.
S2.quote: I'm a wait-and-see person in a picture where waiting means you've already lost.
S2.fieldNote: She recognised that her usual habit of waiting for proof doesn't fit a two-year timeline. Her strong savings and her parents' home keep her short of alarm. Cuts are concrete and ordered around protecting the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to be sensible, if people actually start now. I'd say the company should tell us its plan in year one, not year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it'd hit Marcus around year two or three, and me around year five. I'd still be the one with the job in the middle bit, which means the pressure's on me, the overtime, the night shifts, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every overtime shift I could in the first two years and put it on the mortgage. Once I could see what the robots on the lines actually look like, I'd sign up for whatever course runs them. And I'd push Marcus to retrain early, before the warehouse goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, honestly. A different kind. Longer, slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does five years still feel anxious when two felt the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with two years, you can't do anything, so you just brace. With five, there's time to get it wrong. I'd be the one making the calls, and if I backed the wrong course or the wrong year, that's on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra overtime cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time with Kai and Lily, mostly. Lily's exams would be right in the middle of it. I'd hate missing that. I'd say yes to the shifts and feel guilty every time.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time to be sensible if people start now, and the company should share its plan in year one, not year four.
S3.think: It would hit my partner around year two or three and me around year five, so I'd be the main earner in the middle stretch with all the overtime and night shifts.
S3.do: Takes every overtime shift possible in the first two years and puts it on the mortgage. Signs up for training to run line robots once she sees what they look like, and pushes her partner to retrain before his warehouse automates.
S3.feel: Still anxious, but a longer, slower kind.
S3.quote: With two years, you can't do anything, so you just brace. With five, there's time to get it wrong.
S3.fieldNote: Surprisingly, more time doesn't calm her, because it puts decisions and blame on her shoulders. She'd carry the household during her partner's transition. Overtime would cost her time with her daughter during exams, and she knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair warning, and if we waste it, that's on all of us. I'd be telling the younger ones on the crew to start thinking now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be alright. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage mostly paid, Lily through university and Kai nearly. Marcus would have time to move into something properly. It's not nothing, but it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and keep saving. In a few years, when the line robots are actually being tested, I'd train on them. I'd talk to Lily and Kai about what they study, maybe nudge them away from anything a robot could do, though I don't really know what that is yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. It feels like a long weather warning you can prepare for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you nudge Lily toward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to do psychology. I'd have said fine before. Now I'd say, do it, but make sure you're the kind that sits with people, not the kind that writes reports. I don't know if that's right. I'd just be guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that appeals to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No more nights, maybe. If a robot did the two a.m. call-outs and I got to supervise it from a day shift, I wouldn't say no. I've done enough nights for one life.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning and wasting it would be on all of us, and I'd tell younger crew members to start thinking about it now.
S4.think: We'd be alright, because by fifty-three the mortgage would be mostly paid and the children mostly through education. My partner would have time to move into something properly.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving, then trains on line robots when they start being tested in a few years. Talks with her children about study choices that a robot couldn't easily replace.
S4.feel: Uneasy but not frightened, like a long weather warning you can prepare for.
S4.quote: If a robot did the two a.m. call-outs and I got to supervise it from a day shift, I wouldn't say no.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she finally relaxes, and even sees an upside in escaping night shifts. Her plans are paced to proof, as usual. She openly admits she's guessing about her daughter's studies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. What would help is time, which that one doesn't give. Failing that, some kind of income support while people retrain, and the company telling us its plans honestly and early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Storms. Whatever happens, the sea doesn't stop. The first robot that has to do glove work in sideways rain at the seafront, I'd like to be standing there watching. With a flask.

headlineQuote: The first robot that has to do glove work in sideways rain at the seafront, I'd like to be standing there watching.
portrait: Hana Zhang is a 43-year-old fault and emergency lineworker on a coastal crew, working a day-night rota and doing live-line glove work against salt corrosion and gales. Her partner Marcus manages at a warehouse already trialling robot pickers, so most of her worry runs through his job rather than hers. She uses AI now and then and waits for colleagues to prove tools before relying on them. Fast AGI makes her anxious because waiting no longer works, five years stays anxious because the decisions fall on her, and only ten years feels manageable.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time to prepare and her partner would likely lose his job first.
whatWouldHelp: Income support while people retrain, and her employer sharing its plans honestly and early.
